articles.title: Alberta tables bill giving the province power over city bike lanes
articles.dek: Bill 43 would bar new bike lanes that take road space from vehicles without the transportation minister's approval and let the province order existing lanes removed.
body: The Alberta government tabled legislation on Thursday, Nov. 19, that would give the province control over municipal bike lanes in Calgary, Edmonton and other cities [1][2]. Transportation and Economic Corridors Minister Devin Dreeshen introduced Bill 43, the Safe and Sensible Roads Act 2026 [1][2].

If the bill passes, municipalities could not install a new bike lane that removes or restricts road capacity for vehicles unless the minister gives written approval [1][2]. The minister could also order the removal of existing bike lanes that reduce capacity for motor vehicles, and could return them to vehicle use during road work [2]. Municipalities could ask for exemptions, which would be judged case by case, with the minister making the final decision [2]. The bill sets no criteria for the minister's decisions [1].

Dreeshen said the province will ask Calgary and Edmonton for data on certain bike lanes, including traffic impact assessments of those roads and nearby roads, and then decide with the municipalities whether a lane makes sense [2]. A provincial bike lane portal this summer drew 14,000 responses, and 26 Street in Calgary was among the 10 most-reported lanes; the other nine on the list are in Edmonton [2]. Officials said the bill does not set out an exact removal process [2]. The Canadian Press reported the bill does not say who would pay for removals, while the Edmonton Journal reported that cities would bear the cost [1][2]. Asked about funding, Dreeshen said, "We do not have a provincial bike lane budget" [2].

The bill also covers other transportation matters. It would raise penalties for unsafe commercial trucking operators and create provincial safety standards for privately owned e-scooters, one-wheels and similar personal devices [1][2]. The province is considering helmet rules and possible limits on speed, power and weight, with the standards due in early 2027 and taking effect April 1, 2027; municipalities would keep bylaw authority over how the devices operate [2]. The bill would also align municipal LRT projects with the province's Passenger Rail Master Plan [2].

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas spoke against provincial intervention in bike lanes, and Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack raised concerns about costs passed to taxpayers [1]. Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi told the province to stay out of the issue [2]. Cycling advocates warned that removing lanes would put cyclists at risk [1]. Details are to be set in regulations, which the Canadian Press reported are expected to take effect in the spring [1].
key_facts: Bill 43, the Safe and Sensible Roads Act 2026, tabled Nov. 19
New lanes that take road space from vehicles would need the minister's written approval
26 Street in Calgary was among the 10 most-reported lanes in a provincial portal
E-scooter and personal device standards would take effect April 1, 2027

articles.title: Province's data centre bill sets 600-metre buffer from homes; Calgary councillors call it a good start
articles.dek: Bill 42 would keep large data centres away from homes and top farmland and make the Alberta Utilities Commission their main regulator, a day after Calgary council moved on its own rules.
body: The Alberta government has tabled Bill 42, the Energy, Environment and Utilities Statutes Amendment Act, 2026, which would set province-wide rules for where large data centres can be built [1][2]. Technology and Innovation Minister Nate Glubish tabled the omnibus bill in the legislature on Wednesday, Nov. 18 [1][4].

Under the bill, data centres of 10 megawatts or more could not be built within 600 metres of a home, on irrigated land or on high-quality farmland [1][2][4]. The province says that protects about 14 million acres of farmland [2][4]. Municipalities may set larger setbacks, and the 600-metre distance is a minimum [1][3]. Sites in designated industrial zones, on brownfield land or at existing power plants would not need the setback [1][4]. Projects under 10 megawatts would stay with municipalities [4].

The Alberta Utilities Commission would be the main regulator for data centres of 10 megawatts and up, and would apply the same noise and light standards used for power plants [2][4]. The bill would let the province set water-efficiency standards aimed at bringing cooling water use to near zero, with details to come in regulations [3][4]. Data centre proponents would have to pay for the grid infrastructure they need [2][3]. Officials say 70 proposals are in the province's program and up to 30 per cent could be affected [2][4]. Projects already approved or well underway, including Meta's planned $13-billion campus near Edmonton, would be exempt [1][4]. The bill also covers oil and gas cleanup, illegal dumping penalties and forestry, and repeals the Oil Sands Emissions Limit Act [2].

In Calgary, councillors said the rules could address local concerns about water, power and noise [3]. Council voted on Tuesday to study the effects of large data centres and pursue land-use bylaw changes [3]. Ward 5 Coun. Raj Dhaliwal called the provincial rules a positive step but said they do not replace the city's own due diligence, and he wants a tool to pause emerging industries [3]. Ward 2 Coun. Jennifer Wyness called the rules a great start and welcomed that land-use decisions and public hearings stay with cities, while noting uncertainty about effects on residents and property values [3].

Critics want more. An Olds-area opponent has called for buffers of two to five kilometres [1], and NDP critic Nathan Ip said, "It's unclear if this government has actually consulted with municipalities" [4]. A July Leger poll cited by Global News found Canadians closely split on data centre development in their province [1].
key_facts: Bill 42 tabled Nov. 18 in the Alberta legislature
600-metre minimum buffer for data centres of 10 MW or more
Alberta Utilities Commission would regulate large projects
Calgary council voted Nov. 17 to study data centre impacts and bylaw changes

articles.title: Calgary firefighters handle four fires in 24 hours, including an encampment tent fire
articles.dek: One person was taken to hospital with significant burns after a tent fire in the southeast, and another after a vehicle fire near Stoney Trail.
body: The Calgary Fire Department responded to four fires in about 24 hours on Tuesday, Nov. 17, and early Wednesday, Nov. 18, as heavy, wet snow fell on the city [1][2].

Shortly before 6 a.m. on Tuesday, crews were called to an occupied encampment in the 4400 block of Ogden Road S.E., where a tent was on fire [1][2]. Firefighters knocked the fire down quickly with a hose line [1]. One person, the tent's only occupant, had significant burn injuries and was taken to hospital by EHS after initial treatment [1]. A fire investigator found the fire started inside the tent [1].

Around 7:30 a.m., crews went to a single-vehicle fire off the road near Stoney Trail and Sun Valley Boulevard S.E. [1]. One person was found on the ground and was cared for by firefighters before being taken to hospital [1]. Crews found a damaged electrical vault near the collision and called Enmax to assess it, and the fire department left the scene with Calgary police [1]. A CJWE report placed the vehicle fire on Ashley Crescent, which differs from the fire department's account [2].

Just before 6 p.m., heavy smoke and fire were coming from a bedroom window of a single-storey home in the 300 block of Ashley Crescent S.E. [1][3]. Everyone inside got out on their own, one person was assessed on scene and not taken to hospital, and the fire was kept to the bedroom [1].

Around 4 a.m. Wednesday, a shed or playhouse-type structure at the rear of a property in the 100 block of Rundlehorn Crescent N.E. caught fire [1][2]. The occupants left on their own, the house was not damaged, and crews checked neighbouring garages for heat and damage [1]. No injuries were reported [1].
Investigators attended the house and shed fires [1]. The department used the release to remind families to practise a home escape plan twice a year [1].
key_facts: Four fires between early Tuesday, Nov. 17, and early Wednesday, Nov. 18
Two people taken to hospital: one from a tent fire, one from a vehicle fire
House fire on Ashley Crescent S.E. was contained to a bedroom
No injuries in the Rundlehorn Crescent N.E. shed fire

articles.title: Man faces 15 charges after string of vehicle thefts and break-in attempts, police say
articles.dek: Calgary police say the man breached release conditions while committing thefts between mid-September and late October.
body: Calgary police have laid 15 charges against a 48-year-old man they describe as a prolific offender, following a series of thefts and attempted vehicle break-ins this fall [1][2].

Police say the man was released from custody in May and then breached his release conditions while committing offences between Monday, Sept. 14, and Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026 [1]. The alleged offences included attempted break-ins to vehicles, a theft from a recreation centre office and the use of stolen credit cards [1]. CTV News reported the case involved several car prowlings and thefts between mid-September and mid-October [2].
On Tuesday, Nov. 3, officers saw the man going into unlocked parked vehicles along 17 Avenue S.W. and arrested him, according to police [1].

Jonathan Keith Holmes, 48, is charged with two counts of theft under $5,000, one count of attempted theft under $5,000, two counts of using stolen credit cards, eight counts of breaching a release order, one count of attempted break and enter and one count of possession of a controlled substance [1]. None of the charges has been proven in court.
Police said he remained in custody and was scheduled to next appear in court on Thursday, Nov. 19 [1]. The outcome of that appearance was not available.

Police are asking anyone with information to call the non-emergency line at 403-266-1234 [1]. They also advised drivers to lock their vehicles and remove valuables, including wallets, purses and mail [1].
key_facts: 15 charges, including eight counts of breaching a release order
Alleged offences between Sept. 14 and Oct. 20, 2026
Arrested Nov. 3 along 17 Avenue S.W.
Next court appearance was set for Nov. 19

articles.title: Alberta Teachers' Association says recent education changes are causing 'chaos and confusion'
articles.dek: The teachers' union called for consultation before new legislation as school boards in Calgary wait for details on the new graduation rules.
body: The Alberta Teachers' Association criticized a series of recent provincial education decisions at a news conference on Thursday, Nov. 19, adding a formal union response to the debate over the province's new high school graduation rules [1].

ATA president Jason Schilling described the moves as political distractions [1]. He pointed to Bill 35, introduced in October, on reporting student achievement to families; the former Bill 25 from March on political neutrality in schools; and last week's updated graduation requirements [1]. He said the changes were introduced without consulting those who work in education, and asked for a clear, transparent process before new legislation is brought in [1]. He also urged the public to contact their MLAs [1].

Under the new rules, by 2030 Grade 11 and 12 students would need fewer core credits and have more room for electives [1]. Physical education would be required throughout high school, and a revised career and life management course would be needed to graduate [1]. The ATA raised concerns about literacy gaps and hurdles for students entering post-secondary, as well as staffing and gymnasium space [1].

Education and Childcare Minister Demetrios Nicolaides said on Nov. 13 that the graduation decision was partly informed by his student advisory council [1]. Asked in question period who he consulted, he cited several American research studies [1]. Premier Danielle Smith has defended the changes, while NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said they appeared to lower standards [1].

In Calgary, the Calgary Board of Education said it had not yet received details from the ministry, and the Calgary Catholic School District said it will assess the impacts [1]. No government timeline for further steps was given [1].
key_facts: ATA news conference held Nov. 19
Union cites Bill 35, former Bill 25 and new graduation rules
New rules take full effect by 2030 for Grades 11 and 12
CBE has not yet received ministry details; Calgary Catholic is assessing impacts

articles.title: Flames host the league-leading Wild at the Saddledome on Thursday night
articles.dek: Minnesota arrives on a long point streak, while Calgary seeks a repeat of its 2-1 home win over the Wild in October.
body: The Calgary Flames host the Minnesota Wild at the Scotiabank Saddledome on Thursday, Nov. 19, with puck drop at 6 p.m. Calgary time (7 p.m. Central) [1][2].

Minnesota comes in at 16-3-4 with 36 points, second overall in the NHL [1]. The sources differ on the length of the Wild's run: The Hockey News reported a point in 10 straight games, while the Wild's own preview cited a 12-game point streak and an eight-game road winning streak [1][2]. Kirill Kaprizov ranks third in the league with 40 points, including 17 goals [1].

Calgary is 10-11-1 with 21 points [1]. The Flames beat Minnesota 2-1 at the Saddledome in October, which The Hockey News reported was the Wild's last regulation loss [1]. Goaltender Dustin Wolf was expected to start for Calgary after a win in San Jose [1].

Former Flames forward Blake Coleman returns to the Saddledome for the second time since joining Minnesota, and was listed on the Wild's third line [1][2]. The Wild's projected goaltenders were Jesper Wallstedt and Calvin Pickard, and the team noted its lineup was subject to change [2].
Calgary's projected lines had Joel Farabee, Mikael Backlund and Matt Coronato together on the top unit, with Zayne Parekh and Simon Nemec among the defencemen [1].
key_facts: Wild at Flames, Thursday, Nov. 19, 6 p.m. Calgary time
Minnesota: 16-3-4, 36 points; Calgary: 10-11-1, 21 points
Calgary beat Minnesota 2-1 at the Saddledome in October
Dustin Wolf expected in goal for Calgary
